title: Understanding Performance in Test Taking: The Role of Question Difficulty Order https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S027277572200067X
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 23, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises a field experiment with over 19,000 participants, plus analysis of PISA data, testing how the order of question difficulty within a test affects completion rates and accuracy. The finding is clear: placing easier questions first leads to higher completion rates and more correct answers overall, likely because early difficult questions can discourage students and signal that the whole test will be hard. Barton draws out the practical assessment-design implication — order matters, and it should be chosen deliberately based on what the assessment is trying to measure — while also flagging test fatigue as a separate risk on long or difficult tests. He notes the research is grounded in large-scale standardised testing rather than day-to-day classroom quizzes, so teachers should weigh how directly it transfers to their own assessment design.
points: Placing easier questions at the start of a test measurably increases both completion rates and the number of correct answers overall.
Encountering a hard question early appears to discourage students, potentially by signalling that the rest of the test will be difficult.
Test fatigue is a distinct risk on long assessments; breaks or varied difficulty can help mitigate declining performance on later questions.
The choice of question order should follow the assessment's purpose: easy-to-hard for accurate measurement of general knowledge, a different order if testing resilience under challenge.
quotes: The authors conduct a field experiment with over 19,000 participants and analyze data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) to investigate how the arrangement of questions by difficulty influences test completion rates and accuracy.
Their findings suggest that placing easier questions at the beginning of tests leads to higher completion rates and a greater number of correct answers.
Teachers should consider ordering questions from easiest to most difficult.
Teachers should be aware that students may be discouraged if they encounter a difficult question early in a test.
Teachers should be mindful of the potential impact of test fatigue.
Teachers should be aware that students may be more optimistic about their performance if they encounter easy questions at the beginning of a test.
